status: Eleven lead-approved replacements integrated in existing land slots with eleven new media assets. Five candidates held. No publication.

entries.subject: fennec fox
entries.title: To my face
entries.body: Say it to my face. It makes very little difference acoustically.

replacement.oldBody: Something scratched beneath the sand. I dug until my ears were full of it. The scratching stopped. Now I can hear one grain moving inside my left ear and nothing else worth eating.

image.sceneMatch: Curled fennec with upright oversized ears. The terse challenge depends on visible ear scale.

entries.payoff: Excellent hearing makes the conventional demand acoustically unnecessary.

entries.subject: fennec fox
entries.title: Together
entries.body: We slept together. Sleep was the part we were bad at.

replacement.oldBody: My neighbor chews with his mouth open at the entrance of his burrow. I went over to object and he offered me the last bit. It was very good. I will object again tomorrow.

image.sceneMatch: Two fennecs with tousled coats stand together. Intimacy is fictional, not a claim of observed mating.

entries.payoff: Physical dishevelment supports a compact double meaning.

entries.subject: fennec fox
entries.title: In her footsteps
entries.body:
My mother used to catch one claw on stone. Three soft steps, then a tiny drag.

I heard it this morning. I was on my feet before I remembered how long it had been.

My daughter came around the rock. She had something stuck between her toes. Stopped to pull at it, then came on. Three steps. The little drag.

I told her she was making a terrible noise.

She looked at the open space around us. Looked at me. Put her paw down very carefully.

I went over and got the burr out.

She bounded away without it. I stood there with the burr in my mouth.

replacement.oldBody: A dry root tapped against the sand all night. I pounced on it twice before the wind stopped and showed me what I had been hunting. I carried it away anyway. I need sleep.

image.sceneMatch: Standing adult fennec with visible paws and alert ears. The burr and relatives are a remembered fictional encounter, not pictured.

entries.payoff: A familiar sound briefly restores a lost relationship, then the burr remains after the practical problem is solved.

entries.subject: fennec fox
entries.title: A little space
entries.body: I asked for a little space. They each found a different little space to disappear into. I have withdrawn the request.

replacement.oldBody: I hid a scrap beside a small bush. The wind buried the bush. Found the scrap by smell, but had to dig through a disappointing amount of yesterday to get it.

image.sceneMatch: Adult and three smaller foxes occupy separate openings around a log. Captive setting retained in provenance; family roles are fictional.

entries.payoff: The desired privacy becomes several simultaneous parental worries.

entries.subject: fennec fox
entries.title: Right here
entries.body: He licked my nose and went away. I have been sitting with my nose out ever since. Ridiculous part of the body to miss somebody in.

replacement.oldBody: The sky darkened over my back and I reached the burrow before I had decided to run. Stayed inside until dusk. Spent most of the day pretending I had meant to come home early.

image.sceneMatch: Close face and nose illustrate where remembered affectionate contact lingers. The other fox is unpictured.

entries.payoff: Separation registers in an unexpectedly specific part of the body.

entries.subject: fennec fox
entries.title: The middle
entries.body: Someone's paw is under my ribs. I could move. Then I'd have to find out whether they would move with me.

replacement.oldBody: Lay with my chin on the sand after everyone settled. Tiny feet kept moving underneath. All that dark, full of errands. Then my stomach growled and ruined the small ones.

image.sceneMatch: Several foxes rest tightly against each other. Contact and crowding are visible; a particular hidden paw is fictional.

entries.payoff: The discomfort protects her from a more frightening question about affection.

entries.subject: Philippine tarsier
entries.title: Nearly concealed
entries.body: I can put the trunk between us. I cannot get both eyes behind it without becoming someone considerably narrower.

replacement.oldBody: Leapt to a very thin trunk. It bent, returned, and sent me partway back. I held on through the second opinion.

image.sceneMatch: Tarsier grips a thin stem, with enormous eyes extending widely beside it.

entries.payoff: The usual hiding strategy cannot accommodate her visible eye width.

entries.subject: Philippine tarsier
entries.title: Potential
entries.body: I can jump a very long way. This has given people entirely the wrong idea about my willingness to let go.

replacement.oldBody: The moon came through a gap and lit the leaf I was watching. I could see every vein, every nick, every empty place where a beetle was failing to be.

image.sceneMatch: Fingers and toes grip a narrow branch with textured bark. The apparent reluctance is imagined; moss is not asserted.

provenance.sourceDescription: Philippine Tarsier (Carlito syrichta) hugging a mossy branch. Photo taken at the Tarsier Sanctuary, Corella, Bohol

entries.payoff: Athletic capability does not imply emotional readiness.

entries.subject: Philippine tarsier
entries.title: Casually
entries.body: I tried to look at him casually. These are the smallest eyes I could do.

replacement.oldBody: Felt somebody land before I saw him. He was clinging to the other side of my trunk. We each leaned around to inspect the other and continued seeing only bark.

image.sceneMatch: Close tarsier face with large eyes supports the failed attempt to look casually at another; that animal is unpictured.

entries.payoff: Her anatomy defeats the attempted casual glance.

entries.subject: Philippine tarsier
entries.title: Read ahead
entries.body: I dreamed I had wings. Woke up biting the branch. Apparently some part of me had read ahead.

replacement.oldBody: Picked a closer trunk for my next leap. Landed exactly where I meant to. Nobody was there to appreciate the improvement, so I stayed awhile appreciating it myself.

image.sceneMatch: Tarsier rests its mouth against a branch under foliage. Biting on waking is fictional remembered action, not a claim that teeth are visible.

entries.payoff: The dream's pleasure and the sleeping grip have incompatible expectations.

entries.subject: Philippine tarsier
entries.title: Introductions
entries.body: The leaf keeps touching my ear. I turn to see who's there. Leaf. I turn back. We have been introduced five times.

replacement.oldBody: Rain started on the leaves around me. I turned toward the first noise, then the second, then gave the entire forest a very hard stare.

image.sceneMatch: A broad green leaf hangs close over the tarsier's ear. Repeated contact is fiction, not a recorded movement sequence.

entries.subject: quokka
entries.title: My contribution
entries.body: I have brought nothing to this argument except my whole body. It is blocking the way quite well.

replacement.oldBody: The other quokka took the leaf I was reaching for. I chewed what I had and watched her. My face may have looked friendly. The chewing was extremely pointed.

image.sceneMatch: Quokka stands on bare ground with its rounded body across the view. The argument is fictional and unpictured.

entries.payoff: A soft-looking body is an effective obstruction.

entries.subject: quokka
entries.title: The grass afterward
entries.body: I got up and looked at the flattened grass. That cannot all have been underneath me. There must have been someone else.

replacement.oldBody: Climbed into a shrub for a fresh shoot. Ate it, looked down, and discovered that the shoot had been the only part of my plan involving that height.

image.sceneMatch: Round quokka sits in grass. Remembered flattened grass after rising is fictional, not a measured footprint in the picture.

entries.subject: quokka
entries.title: A minute
entries.body: She asked whether I had a minute. I had a leaf. I finished it slowly so I could give her a better answer.

replacement.oldBody: The shade was just wide enough until the sun moved. Pulled my foot in. The other foot went out. I am beginning to understand why the larger quokka arrived before me.

image.sceneMatch: Quokka has an actual green leaf at its mouth amid dry litter. A visitor's question is invented.

entries.subject: quokka
entries.title: Ready
entries.body: He said come as you are. I am standing here as I am. It has taken longer than I expected.

replacement.oldBody: Started a stem from the wrong end and kept chewing because I had started. My jaw got tired. Put it down with the good end facing me for when I become sensible.

image.sceneMatch: Quokka stands facing outward beneath a shrub, forepaws gathered at its chest. The invitation is fictional.

entries.payoff: An uncomplicated invitation creates awkward anticipation.

entries.subject: quokka
entries.title: Across my face
entries.body:
She used to fit underneath my chin.

Now she climbs across my face on the way to things. Puts a foot on my cheek, hauls the rest of herself over, and leaves me to work out which way my whiskers used to point.

I could get up. There is plenty of room under the tree. I think about that every time she crosses me.

This afternoon she went around instead. She had found another place to lie down, a little farther into the shade. I stretched out. Put my head where I wanted it. Nobody stepped on anything.

After a while I got up and went to her.

I was aiming to lie alongside. Misjudged the gap. Put my foot on her face.

She made exactly the noise I make.

replacement.oldBody: Found another excellent shoot above my head. Climbed, ate, and came down backward this time. Stood at the bottom chewing very slowly in case anyone wanted to ask about my technique.

image.sceneMatch: Young quokka leans across a reclining adult beneath a tree. Maternal roles and remembered reciprocal foot contact are fictional.
